nameStory: The "fringed kidney lichen" gets its name from its kidney-shaped lobes with delicately fringed edges that look like tiny lace trim. The "kidney" part comes from the distinctive rounded, bean-like shape of its leaf-like segments, while "fringed" describes the fine, hair-like projections along the margins that give it an almost fuzzy appearance.
description: Fringed kidney lichen is a leafy (foliose) lichen that forms distinctive kidney-shaped lobes with delicate, fringed edges. It's a cyanolichen, meaning it partners with blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) instead of the more common green algae. This partnership gives it a unique ability to fix nitrogen from the air. The lobes can grow several inches across and have a soft, almost velvety texture when dry.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms distinctive kidney or bean-shaped lobes that are loosely attached to the substrate, feeling soft and pliable like thin leather when moist

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Edges are distinctly fringed with fine, hair-like projections that you can see and feel - run your finger gently along the margin to detect the soft fringe

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray-green to brownish when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet, with the underside typically lighter colored

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Found on tree bark, particularly in moist areas where humidity stays high, occasionally on rocks in very humid locations

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes can reach 2-4 inches across, forming loose colonies that may cover substantial areas of trunk or branch

habitat: In New England, look for this rare lichen in the moistest, shadiest spots of old-growth or mature forests, especially near streams, waterfalls, or in deep ravines where humidity stays consistently high. It prefers the lower trunks of deciduous trees in areas with coastal influence or other sources of reliable moisture. You're most likely to find it in protected valleys or north-facing slopes where the air rarely dries out completely.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant after spring rains when the lobes are fully hydrated and show their brightest green colors. The soft texture is most apparent when touched during moist spring weather.
seasonality.summer: May appear more gray-brown and contracted during dry periods, but becomes lush and green again after summer thunderstorms. The fringed edges are still visible even when dry.
seasonality.fall: Often looks its best during the humid fall months when morning dew and frequent rains keep it consistently moist. Colors remain stable as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Visible year-round but may appear darker and more contracted. Snow and winter moisture can rehydrate it, bringing back the characteristic green tones and soft texture.

funFact: This lichen is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only twice by citizen scientists, making it one of the most elusive lichens in the region - finding one would be like discovering a botanical treasure!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other kidney lichens in the Nephroma genus, but the distinctive fringed edges are the key difference - other kidney lichens have smooth or slightly wavy margins, while fringed kidney lichen has those unmistakable hair-like projections you can actually feel with your fingertip.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "helveticum" (meaning "of Switzerland"), this lichen is actually extremely rare in Europe and more commonly found in North America. The scientific understanding of this species has recently changed due to DNA studies showing that what we used to call one species is actually two different ones.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives like powdery kidney lichen and naked kidney lichen, fringed kidney lichen is the only one with those distinctive hair-like fringes along the lobe edges. Powdery kidney lichen has a dusty, powdery surface coating, while naked kidney lichen has smooth, unfringed margins and typically grows in drier conditions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Powdery Kidney Lichen is smaller and more powdery than its relatives in the Nephroma genus.
Unlike its relatives in the kidney lichen group, Mustard Kidney Lichen has a distinctly smooth upper surface and yellowish coloration.
Unlike Powdery Kidney Lichen which is covered in soredia (powdery reproductive structures) that rub off on your fingers, Naked Kidney Lichen has a completely smooth, clean surface.
